html:
Athabaskan (also Athabascan or Dene) is a large family of Native American languages and the peoples who speak them. The map uses the label for the Dene lands of interior Alaska and northwestern Canada in the 1700s; the same peoples appear as Athabaskan on earlier maps.

The family has three groups:

  • Northern: interior Alaska and western Canada, from the Gwich'in to the Chipewyan, whose language covers more ground than any other native language of North America.
  • Pacific Coast: small groups in Oregon and California.
  • Southern or Apachean: the Navajo and Apache, who moved far south to the American Southwest a few centuries before the Spanish arrived.

The name comes from a Cree word for Lake Athabasca. With the distant Eyaq and Tlingit, Athabaskan forms the Na-Dene family, and some linguists link it to the Ket language of Siberia. In the north, Dene hunters traded furs with the Hudson's Bay Company across Rupert's Land.
